notes: Story beat per the brief: the same evening; Philesia measures the stores before a guest arrives; the hare grows in the telling; Gryllus slips out to Sosias in the stable; Sosias admits the dangers of river crossings but will not tell the story; one clue only (Anab. 5.3.8: a Selinus also flows past the Artemision at Ephesus); the boys' questions and the expected stranger are the hook for Κεφάλαιον 3.

Nothing about the Megabyzus deposit, the purchase of the land, or why the river has the name. Per Anab. 5.3.8 the river already had it (ἔτυχε δὲ διαρρέων); Diodorus's guess that his father named it is deliberately wrong and is left for Part III.
Edition conventions as in Κεφάλαιον 1: capital only at a paragraph start and at the start of direct speech; «» for speech; movable ν before a vowel and at a pause.

All five genitive uses of the Μάθημα occur at least twice in the prose: possession s002, s014, s026, s030, s043; part s004, s009, s038; separation s018, s022, s031, s039, s054, s062; comparison s008, s009, s034, s057; time within which s005, s032, s064, s065. No preview markers: the genitive is Athenaze-known (brief).

cover.alt: Evening in a lamplit storeroom lined with big clay jars. A woman with keys at her belt holds a small measuring jug over an open wine jar and looks sideways, unconvinced, at a boy who flings his arms wide as he talks. A smaller boy beside him, the hem of his tunic wet, shakes his head and holds his hands a little apart; a tawny hound sits at his feet. A bearded man leans in the doorway, smiling and saying nothing.
cover.art_brief: Evening of the same spring day as Unit 1, just after nightfall, indoors. The storeroom of the farmhouse at Scillus: whitewashed mudbrick walls, beaten-earth floor, a low wooden ceiling beam; lit by two small clay oil lamps on a ledge (warm orange light, soft deep shadows, still clearly readable). Along the back wall three big clay storage jars (pithoi) half-sunk in the floor and a short row of pointed wine amphorae leaning in a wooden rack; in the foreground two open baskets heaped with pale barley grain. LEFT/CENTRE: Philesia (FIRST APPEARANCE; reference sheet needed), Xenophon's wife, about 35: tall, upright, brisk; dark brown hair parted in the middle and bound in a knot at the nape with a woven band; strong straight brows, a direct, amused, sceptical look; an ankle-length belted chiton of undyed linen and a saffron-ochre wool himation over the left shoulder; a bunch of bronze keys on a cord at her belt. She stands by an open pithos of wine, holding a small clay measuring jug (she is measuring what wine is left), head turned towards the boys with one eyebrow raised. RIGHT: Gryllus (12, madder-red chiton, thick slightly wavy very dark brown hair swept back) in mid-story, arms flung wide to show an enormous hare; beside him Diodorus (10, woad-blue chiton, chestnut curls) shaking his head, holding his hands only a short distance apart (the hare was small); the hem and lower half of Diodorus's chiton visibly dark and wet (he fell in the river). The tawny hound Alke (red collar) sits at Diodorus's feet. BACKGROUND: in the doorway to the dark courtyard, Xenophon (45, oatmeal chiton, dark green chlamys, staff) leans on the frame, silent, with a faint smile. Camera at eye level from inside the room. Same character designs as Unit 1; watercolour-and-ink; no text, no letters on jars.

inference_aids.alt: A stable at night lit by a clay lamp. Three horses stand with their heads at a wooden manger. An old man in a fox-skin cap pours barley from a basket into the manger without stopping, his face half turned to an eager boy who looks up at him and asks a question. A black hound and a brindled hound lie curled in the straw at the old man's feet.
inference_aids.art_brief: Same evening, a little later, the stable (ἱππών) a short way below the house [?]: low walls of fieldstone and mudbrick, a timber roof, straw on the floor, a long wooden manger along the back wall. One clay oil lamp in a wall niche gives warm light; the open doorway at the side shows a dark blue night sky. Three horses (bay, chestnut, grey; ordinary Greek horses, no saddles) stand side by side with their heads down at the manger. CENTRE: Sosias (about 60, Thracian, grey beard, big nose, fox-skin cap with ear flaps and red-and-black zigzag band, patterned brown Thracian cloak, fawn-skin boots) is pouring barley grain from a flat wicker basket into the manger, still working, his face half turned to the boy with a wry, closed expression (he will not tell). Beside him Gryllus (12, madder-red chiton, thick slightly wavy very dark brown hair) stands close, eager, looking up at Sosias with a question. At Sosias's feet, curled in the straw, the black hound Psyche and the brindled hound Thymos (Alke is NOT here: she stayed at the house with Diodorus). Camera at eye level from the far end of the stable, so both faces are readable. Watercolour-and-ink; same character designs as Unit 1; no text.

grammar.note_en:
The genitive. In Κεφάλαιον 1 the genitive answered πόθεν; after ἐκ and ἀπό. Without a preposition it does five common jobs, and this evening uses all five. English needs a word for each ("of", "from", "than", "within"); Greek needs only the case.

1. Possession: whose? ἡ τοῦ Ξενοφῶντος γυνή, "Xenophon's wife" (s002). Here the possessive genitive stands between the article and its noun, where an adjective would; it can also follow the noun, as in τὰ ἐπιτήδεια τοῦ στρατεύματος (s030). With εἰμί it says whose a thing is: οὗτος ὁ λόγος οὐκ ἐμός ἐστιν, ἀλλὰ τοῦ πατρός σου, "this story is not mine but your father's" (s026). ἐμός and τοῦ πατρός do the same job there.

2. Part: of what whole? τοῦ δὲ οἴνου ὀλίγον λοιπόν ἐστιν, "there is little left of the wine" (s004). The whole goes in the genitive; the part (ὀλίγον, πολλοί, a number, a superlative) takes whatever case the sentence needs: πολλοὶ ἡμῶν, "many of us" (s038), μικρότατος τῶν λαγῶν, "the smallest of hares" (s009). A partitive genitive normally stands outside the article–noun group.

3. Separation: from what? Verbs of being away, stopping and lacking take a plain genitive: ὁ ἱππὼν ὀλίγον ἀπεῖχε τῆς οἰκίας, "the stable was a little way from the house" (s018); οὐκ ἐπαύσατο τοῦ ἔργου, "he did not stop his work" (s022); Philesia's παύσασθε τῶν λόγων (s062). δέομαι "need" belongs here: στράτευμα πολλῶν δεῖται, "an army needs many things" (s031). In Κεφάλαιον 1 the same verb meant "beg", with the person in the genitive (δεόμεθά σου). It is the genitive that ἐκ and ἀπό take, without the preposition.

4. Comparison: than what? After a comparative the thing compared goes in the genitive: μείζων ἦν τῆς κυνός, "it was bigger than the hound" (s008); μείζονας τοῦ Σελινοῦντος (s034). Greek can also say ἤ "than" and put both things in the same case: μείζων ἢ ἡ κύων. The genitive is the usual choice when the second thing would be nominative or accusative.

5. Time within which: τριῶν ἡμερῶν ἥξει, "he will come within three days" (s005, again in s064); ἑκάστης ἡμέρας, "each day" (s032); τῆς νυκτός, "during the night" (s065). The other cases mark time differently: the dative says on which day (τῇ τρίτῃ ἡμέρᾳ), and the accusative says for how long (τρεῖς ἡμέρας). The genitive names the stretch of time inside which something happens.

Finding the genitive. Every genitive plural ends in -ων. The usual singular endings, the ones in the table, are -ου (2nd declension, and 1st-declension men's names like Σωσίου), -ας or -ης (1st), and -ος or -ους (3rd). A few nouns have their own: λαγώς, λαγώ (Κεφάλαιον 1), and later πόλις, πόλεως. In the 3rd declension the nominative hides the stem, so the genitive is learned with the noun: κύων, κυνός; παῖς, παιδός; πατήρ, πατρός; στράτευμα, στρατεύματος. That is why the word list gives every noun with its genitive. The second table is for looking things up during the exercises, not for learning by heart.

parergon.title: γάρ
parergon.body_en: γάρ gives the reason for what was just said, or explains it. It is postpositive: normally second in its clause, sometimes later; English "for" moves to the front, or becomes "you see", "because", or a colon. Philesia measures the wine because ξένος γάρ τις τριῶν ἡμερῶν ἥξει, "a guest is coming, you see" (s005). Gryllus slipped out unseen: ἡ γὰρ Φιλησία … οὐκ ᾔσθετο, "for Philesia did not notice" (s017). Sosias sends him off: νὺξ γάρ ἐστιν (s047). In an answer, γάρ can supply the reason asked for: «Διὰ τί;» «Πολλάκις γὰρ οἱ πολέμιοι …» (s036–s037).

pair.sense_grc: διὰ τοῦ ποταμοῦ βαίνω, ἀπὸ τῆς μιᾶς γῆς εἰς τὴν πέραν (+ acc.: διέβη τὸν ποταμόν)
ἐκ τοῦ ὕδατος βαίνω: ὁ Διόδωρος ἔπεσεν εἰς τὸν ποταμόν, εὐθὺς δὲ ἐξέβη
pair.sense_en: step out, get out (of the water, of a boat)

families.spelling_note: ἐκ becomes ἐξ before a vowel, and the augment is a vowel: ἐκ-βαίνω, but ἐξ-έβην, ἐξ-εβαίνομεν (s012, s037). δια- drops its α before the augment: δι-έβητε (s033). Sosias puts the pair side by side: διαβαίνειν μὲν χαλεπὸν ἦν, ἐκβαίνειν δὲ χαλεπώτερον (s035). Crossing is the whole way over; ἐκ- is only the last step, out of the water onto the bank.

diagram.alt: Two panels of a river seen from above. Top, labelled διαβαίνω: a line of footprints goes from one bank straight across the water to the other bank. Bottom, labelled ἐκβαίνω: ripples in the middle of the river where someone fell, and footprints leading only out of the water up onto the near bank.

vocabulary.current_sense: know how to (+ inf.); know, understand
step out, get out (of water, of a boat)
be in danger (of + inf.); be likely to (+ inf.)
stop (+ acc.); mid. παύομαι stop, cease from (+ gen.)
have come, be here; fut. ἥξω will arrive
big, great; comp. μείζων, sup. μέγιστος
